'''Corona''' is a [[neighborhood]] in the [[Borough (New York City)|borough]] of [[Queens]] in [[New York City]]. It borders [[Flushing, Queens|Flushing]] and [[Flushing Meadows–Corona Park]] to the east, [[Jackson Heights, Queens|Jackson Heights]] and  [[Elmhurst, Queens|Elmhurst]] to the west, [[Forest Hills, Queens|Forest Hills]] and [[Rego Park, Queens|Rego Park]] to the south, and [[East Elmhurst, Queens|East Elmhurst]] to the north. Corona's main thoroughfares include Corona Avenue, [[Roosevelt Avenue]], [[New York State Route 25A|Northern Boulevard]], [[Junction Boulevard]], and 108th Street.

Corona has a [[multicultural]] population with a [[Latin Americans|Latino]] majority, and is the site of historic [[African-American]] and [[Italian-American]] communities. After World War II, the majority of the neighborhood's residents were mostly [[Italians|Italian]], [[Germans|German]], [[Irish people|Irish]] and of other European ancestries. Corona also has a significant [[Chinese people in New York City|Chinese]] population.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.msaag.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/13_McGlinn.pdf|title=Beyond Chinatown: Dual immigration and the Chinese population of metropolitan New York City, 2000, pp. 114-115|author=Lawrence A. McGlinn, Department of Geography SUNY-New Paltz|publisher=Middle States Geographer, 2002, 35: 110–119, Journal of the Middle States Division of the Association of American Geographers|access-date=March 7, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402151518/http://msaag.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/13_McGlinn.pdf|archive-date=April 2, 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Corona is mostly part of [[Queens Community Board 4|Queens Community District 4]].<ref name="NYCPlanning4"/> The section north of Roosevelt Avenue, known as '''North Corona''', is the northern section of Corona and is in [[Queens Community Board 3|Community District 3]].<ref name="NYCPlanning3"/> Corona is patrolled by the 110th and 115th Precincts of the [[New York City Police Department]].<ref name="NYPD 110th Precinct"/>

==History==
The area was originally known as West Flushing, but various theories have arisen for its etymology. One theory is that it was renamed by music producer [[Benjamin W. Hitchcock]], a developer who renamed the area in 1872 and sold off land for residential development.<ref name=newsday20080224/> Another theory is that [[real estate developer]] Thomas Waite Howard, who became the first postmaster in 1872,<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1872/06/25/archives/newyork-and-suburban-news-newyork-brooklyn-long-island-westchester.html|title=New-York and Suburban News.; New-York. Brooklyn. Long Island. Westchester County. Staten Island.|date=1872-06-25|work=The New York Times|access-date=2020-03-29|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> petitioned to have the post office name changed to Corona in 1870, suggesting that it was the "crown of Queens County".<ref>{{cite book|last=Antos|first=J.D.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_DbB9BPWr1EC|title=Flushing|publisher=Arcadia Publishing Incorporated|year=2010|isbn=978-1-4396-2364-0|series=Then and Now|page=52|access-date=2020-03-29}}</ref> A third theory is that the name Corona derives from the [[crown]] used as an emblem by the Crown Building Company, which is said to have developed the area. The Italian [[immigrants]] who moved into the new housing stock referred to the neighborhood by the [[Italian language|Italian]] or [[Spanish language|Spanish]] word for "crown", or ''corona''.

Corona was a late-19th-century [[residential development]] in the northeastern corner of the old Town of Newtown. Real estate [[speculator]]s from New York started the community in 1854, the same year that the [[New York and Flushing Railroad]] began service to the area largely to serve a newly opened race course. It was at the [[Fashion Course]] in 1858 that the first games of [[baseball]] to charge admission took place.<ref name=newsday20080224>{{Cite news|first=Claudia|last=Gryvatz Copquin|date=2008-02-24|title=The Neighborhoods of Queens: Corona|pages=18|work=Newsday|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/79549851/the-neighborhoods-of-queens-corona/|access-date=2021-06-14}}</ref> The games, which took place between the All Stars of [[Brooklyn]] and the All Stars of [[Manhattan|New York]], are commonly believed to be the first all-star baseball games and in essence the birthplace of professional baseball. A trophy baseball from this tournament sold in 2005 for nearly $500,000.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.robertedwardauctions.com/auction/2005/1.html |title=1858 Fashion Course Game Trophy Baseball|website=Robert Edwards Auctions|date=2005|access-date=August 5, 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130513015421/http://www.robertedwardauctions.com/auction/2005/1.html |archive-date=May 13, 2013 }} Accessed August 5, 2013</ref><ref>[http://www.baseball-almanac.com/treasure/autont2006b.shtml The 1858 Fashion Race Course Baseball Match] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220829165850/https://www.baseball-almanac.com/treasure/autont2006b.shtml |date=August 29, 2022 }} ''Baseball Almanac''. Accessed August 5, 2013.</ref>

During the second half of the 1940s through the 1960s, many legendary [[African-American]] musicians, civil rights leaders and athletes moved to the neighborhood.<ref name=newsday20080224/> In the last half of the 20th century, Corona saw dramatic [[ethnic succession]]s. In the 1950s, what was predominantly an [[Italian-American]] and [[African-American neighborhood]] began to give way to an influx of [[Dominican American|Dominicans]]. In the late 1990s, Corona saw a new wave of immigrants from [[Latin America]]. The area north of Roosevelt Avenue contained the heart of the historic African-American community. The intersection of 108th Street and Corona Avenue is the historic center of the Italian-American community, sometimes referred to as Corona Heights. The majority Hispanic community now consists of Dominicans, [[Colombian Americans|Colombians]], [[Ecuadorian Americans|Ecuadorians]], [[Salvadoran Americans|Salvadorans]], [[Guatemalan Americans|Guatemalans]], [[Bolivian Americans|Bolivians]], [[Peruvian Americans|Peruvians]], [[Mexican Americans|Mexicans]], [[Venezuelan Americans|Venezuelans]], and [[Chilean Americans|Chileans]]. There are also [[Asian Americans]] ([[Chinese Americans|Chinese]], [[Indian Americans|Indians]], [[Korean Americans|Koreans]], [[Filipino Americans|Filipinos]], and [[Japanese Americans|Japanese]]) as well as Italian Americans and African Americans.{{citation needed|date=January 2023}}

==Structures==
[[File:Igreja Adventista Luso-Brasileira 96-11 34th Av jeh.jpg|thumb|right|250px|Brazilian Adventist Church]]

Dorie Miller Residential Cooperative, built in 1952, comprises six buildings, containing 300 apartments, with 1,300 rooms in total. The cooperative is named after [[Doris Miller|Doris "Dorie" Miller]], a U.S. Naval hero at [[Pearl Harbor]] and the first African-American recipient of the [[Navy Cross]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.pearlharbor.org/dorie-miller.asp |title=Doris "Dorie" Miller bio |access-date=June 8, 2009 |archive-date=June 19, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090619102550/http://www.pearlharbor.org/dorie-miller.asp |url-status=live }}</ref> Among its original residents were jazz greats [[Nat Adderley]] & [[Jimmy Heath]]; Kenneth and Corien Drew, publishers of Queens' first African-American newspaper, ''The Corona East Elmhurst News'', Thelma E. Harris founder of Aburi Press and prominent Queens Judge Henry A. Slaughter. Corona was also the childhood home of [[Marie Maynard Daly]], the first African-American woman to earn a Ph.D. in chemistry.

The [[Louis Armstrong House]] attracts visitors to the neighborhood and preserves the legacy of musician [[Louis Armstrong]], one of Corona's most prominent historical residents.<ref name="newsday20080224"/> It was designated a [[National Historic Landmark]] in 1976.<ref name="nris">{{NRISref|version=2010a}}</ref>[[File:Lemon Ice King of Corona 52 Av 108 St jeh.jpg|thumb|right|250px|Lemon Ice King in Corona]][[The Lemon Ice King of Corona]], an [[Ice cream parlor|ices shop]], is located at 52nd Avenue, Corona Avenue, and 108th Street. Founded in 1944 by Peter Benfaremo, it is a neighborhood point of interest.<ref name="McLogan 2018">{{cite web|url=https://newyork.cbslocal.com/2018/05/21/sampling-the-classics-at-the-lemon-ice-king-of-corona/|title=What To Order At The Lemon Ice King Of Corona|last=McLogan|first=Elle|date=May 21, 2018|website=CBS New York|access-date=January 19, 2020}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{cite web|url=https://www.amny.com/eat-and-drink/lemon-ice-king-of-corona-1-34978098/|title=The Lemon Ice King of Corona has roots in a Queens garage|last=Iseman|first=Courtney|date=August 13, 2019|website=amNewYork|access-date=January 19, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20150909/corona/street-renaming-for-lemon-ice-king-of-corona-approved-by-community-board|title=Street Renaming for Lemon Ice King of Corona Approved by Community Board|last=Honan|first=Katie|date=September 9, 2015|website=DNAinfo New York|access-date=January 20, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181213181530/https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20150909/corona/street-renaming-for-lemon-ice-king-of-corona-approved-by-community-board/|archive-date=December 13, 2018|url-status=dead}}</ref> The shop attracts international tourists due to having been featured in the opening credits of the TV show ''[[The King of Queens]]''.<ref name=":0"/>

Corona used to have three [[kettle pond]]s. One of them, Linden Pond, was located a block south of [[103rd Street–Corona Plaza station]] and was the centerpiece of [[Linden Park (Queens)|Park of the Americas]], located near the original center of Corona.<ref name="Kadinsky2016">{{Cite Hidden Waters NYC|page=}}</ref>{{rp|142}} The pond had become a public health hazard by the early 20th century,<ref>{{cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/clip/42612291/|title=Lake a Menace to Health|date=March 19, 1909|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|access-date=January 20, 2020|page=3|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com {{open access}}}}</ref> and was renovated in 1912;<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/42615313/|title=Linden Park "Clean-Up"|date=May 15, 1913|work=Brooklyn Times-Union|access-date=January 15, 2020|page=8|via=newspapers.com {{open access}}}}</ref> it was removed altogether when the park was renovated in 1947.<ref name="Kadinsky2016"/>{{rp|142}}<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1947/10/01/archives/linden-park-queens-rebuilt.html|title=Linden Park, Queens, Rebuilt|date=1947-10-01|work=The New York Times|access-date=2020-01-19|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> The second was Shady Lake, located at what is now the intersection of 53rd Avenue, Corona Avenue, and 108th Street. The pond, originally used to harvest ice, was drained in the 20th century;<ref name="Kadinsky2016"/>{{Rp|143}} the Lemon Ice King of Corona and William F. Moore Park are now located near the site.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/william-f-moore-park/history|title=William F Moore Park Highlights : NYC Parks|date=June 26, 1939|website=New York City Department of Parks & Recreation|access-date=January 20, 2020}}</ref> A third, Backus Lake at 98th Street and 31st Avenue, was also considered a nuisance by the 1900s,<ref>{{cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/clip/42615795/|title=Object to Pond|date=August 31, 1909|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|access-date=January 20, 2020|page=6|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com {{open access}}}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://fultonhistory.com/Newspaper4/Newtown%20NY%20Register/Newtown%20NY%20Register%201911%20Grayscale/Newtown%20NY%20Register%201911%20Grayscale%20-%200032.pdf|title=That Backus Pond|date=January 12, 1911|work=Newtown Register|page=8|via=fultonhistory.com|access-date=January 15, 2020}}</ref> and was drained in 1917.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://hiddenwatersblog.wordpress.com/2016/01/04/backus-pond-queens/|title=Backus' Pond, Queens|last=Kadinsky|first=Sergey|date=January 4, 2016|website=Hidden Waters|access-date=January 20, 2020}}</ref>

===Corona Plaza===
[[File:103 St- Corona Plaza.jpg|alt=Open street plaza with elevated subway line at the left of the photo and vendor booths surrounding the plaza selling shirts and other items.|thumb|People walking around Corona Plaza in the morning, fall 2026]]
Corona Plaza, located at Roosevelt Avenue and National Street, was previously an underutilized lot and truck route that was transformed over the course of several years into a pedestrian [[plaza]] for community programming and inclusive living. In the latter half of the 20th century, the area that is now Corona Plaza was a lot that connected the street to a row of mainly immigrant-owned businesses. The neighborhood of Corona had an overflow of immigrants who struggled to find employment which exacerbated illegal trading, much of which would occur through the use of trucks that could park in this unofficial lot. By the early 21st century, Corona Plaza was gradually given more attention and became a [[Community centre|community space]] for the ethnically diverse population of Corona.<ref name="ScienceDirect">{{cite journal|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877916617300425|title=Re-envisioning community spaces in Corona, Queens, New York City|last1=Taylor|first1=Johanna K.|journal=City, Culture and Society|year=2018 |volume=14 |pages=14–21 |publisher=ELSEVIER|doi=10.1016/j.ccs.2017.12.004 |s2cid=159029071 |access-date=4 November 2019|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

In 2005, the nearby [[Queens Museum]] began applying for permits to temporarily close off the streets that allowed vehicle access to the plaza and hosted public events (typically art based) that the residents of the community could attend.<ref name="queensmuseum">{{cite web |title=Corona Plaza |url=https://queensmuseum.org/corona-plaza |website=Queensmuseum |publisher=Queens Museum |access-date=4 November 2019}}</ref> Seeing the lot's future potential, the Queens Museum partnered with the [[New York City Economic Development Corporation|Queens Economic Development Corporation]] (QEDC) to develop plans to reuse the space.<ref name="ScienceDirect"/> The partners saw this as an opportunity for grassroots, art-led engagement that would unite residents. The two groups' individual intentions both contributed to the creation of the permanent plaza: the QEDC supports developing local businesses while the Queens Museum creates a stronger presence in the neighborhood for its arts programs,<ref name="ScienceDirect"/>

The space was first transformed in 2012 as a temporary plaza with chairs and tables that prohibited through traffic. It was later made permanent by the [[New York City Department of Design and Construction|Department of Design and Construction]], which filled in the lot with concrete, added built-in seating and a performance space, new pedestrian lighting, and plants to reinforce the liveliness. Later added was a drinking fountain, WalkNYC wayfinding signs, bike racks to serve commuters, an automatic [[pay toilet]], and more furniture.<ref name="QNS">{{cite web |last1=Matua |first1=Angela |date=April 11, 2017 |title=City begins a $5.6 million transformation of Corona Plaza into a lively public space |url=https://qns.com/story/2017/04/11/city-begins-5-6-million-transformation-corona-plaza-lively-public-space/ |website=QNS |access-date=4 November 2019}}</ref> Maintenance and technical assistance (including daily cleaning) services for the plaza are funded by the [[New York City Department of Transportation]] (NYCDOT),<ref name="NYCDOT">{{cite web |last1=Michaels |first1=Ian |title=NYC DOT, NYC DDC, Council Member Ferreras-Copeland, and Partners Celebrate Groundbreaking of the Newly Designed Corona Plaza |url=https://www1.nyc.gov/site/ddc/about/press-releases/2017/pr-041017-corona-plaza.page |website=NYC.gov |publisher=Department of Design and Construction |access-date=4 November 2019}}</ref> which has also partnered with the Queens Museum to bring programming to the newly transformed space. The plaza was fully implemented in early 2018 at a cost of around $5.6 million.<ref name="NYCDOT"/> Corona Plaza is recognized by [[urban planning]] circles as a project that has created a new community space.

==Demographics==

According to the [[2010 United States census|2010 census]], the total population of Corona was about 110,000.<ref>[http://www.nyc.gov/html/dcp/pdf/census/census2010/t_pl_p1_nta.pdf Table PL-P1 NTA: Total Population New York City Neighborhood Tabulation Areas, 2010] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131017183129/http://www.nyc.gov/html/dcp/pdf/census/census2010/t_pl_p1_nta.pdf |date=October 17, 2013 }}</ref> Corona's population is overwhelmingly Hispanic; all other demographic groups (Asian, non-Hispanic black, and non-Hispanic white) form a significantly smaller share than they do for the borough as a whole.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://quickfacts.census.gov/qfd/states/36/36081lk.html|title=Queens County, New York QuickLinks|publisher=U.S. Census Bureau|access-date=February 16, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160225014329/http://quickfacts.census.gov/qfd/states/36/36081lk.html|archive-date=February 25, 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Corona is divided into two neighborhood tabulation areas, Corona (south of Roosevelt Avenue) and North Corona (north of Roosevelt Avenue), which collectively comprise the population of the greater neighborhood.<ref>[https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/ntas.pdf New York City Neighborhood Tabulation Areas*, 2010] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181129141839/https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/ntas.pdf |date=November 29, 2018 }}, Population Division - [[New York City]] Department of City Planning, February 2012. Accessed June 16, 2016.</ref>

===Corona===
Based on data from the [[2010 United States census]], the population of Corona south of Roosevelt Avenue was 57,658, a change of 5,576 (9.7%) from the 52,082 counted in [[2000 United States census|2000]]. Covering an area of {{Cvt|462.74|acre}}, the neighborhood had a population density of {{convert|124.6|PD/acre|PD/sqmi PD/sqkm}}.<ref name="PLP5">[http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p5_nta.pdf Table PL-P5 NTA: Total Population and Persons Per Acre - New York City Neighborhood Tabulation Areas*, 2010] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160610175331/http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p5_nta.pdf |date=June 10, 2016 }}, Population Division - [[New York City]] Department of City Planning, February 2012. Accessed June 16, 2016.</ref>

The [[Race and ethnicity in the United States census|racial makeup]] of the neighborhood was 8.4% (4,851) White, 13.6% (7,845) Black, 0.2% (130) Native American, 12.7% (7,346) Asian, 0% (9) Pacific Islander, 0.5% (280) from [[Race (United States Census)|other races]], and 1.3% (723) from two or more races. Hispanic or Latino of any race were 63.3% (36,474) of the population.<ref name="PLP3A">[http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p3a_nta.pdf Table PL-P3A NTA: Total Population by Mutually Exclusive Race and Hispanic Origin - New York City Neighborhood Tabulation Areas*, 2010] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160610170733/http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p3a_nta.pdf |date=June 10, 2016 }}, Population Division - [[New York City]] Department of City Planning, March 29, 2011. Accessed June 14, 2016.</ref>

The entirety of Community Board 4, which comprises Corona and Elmhurst, had 135,972 inhabitants as of [[NYC Health]]'s 2018 Community Health Profile, with an average life expectancy of 85.4 years.<ref name="CHP2018">{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/data/2018chp-qn4.pdf|title=Elmhurst and Corona (Including Corona, Corona Heights, Elmhurst and Lefrak City)|date=2018|website=nyc.gov|publisher=NYC Health|access-date=March 2, 2019}}</ref>{{Rp|2, 20}} This is higher than the median life expectancy of 81.2 for all New York City neighborhoods.<ref name=":21">{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/tcny/community-health-assessment-plan.pdf|title=2016-2018 Community Health Assessment and Community Health Improvement Plan: Take Care New York 2020|date=2016|website=[[government of New York City|nyc.gov]]|publisher=[[New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene]]|access-date=September 8, 2017}}</ref>{{Rp|53 (PDF p. 84)}}<ref>{{cite web | title=New Yorkers are living longer, happier and healthier lives | website=New York Post | date=June 4, 2017 | url=https://nypost.com/2017/06/04/new-yorkers-are-living-longer-happier-and-healthier-lives/ | access-date=March 1, 2019}}</ref> Most inhabitants are middle-aged adults and youth: 17% are between the ages of 0–17, 39% between 25 and 44, and 24% between 45 and 64. The ratio of college-aged and elderly residents was lower, at 8% and 12%, respectively.<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{Rp|2}}

As of 2017, the median [[household income]] in Community Board 4 was $51,992.<ref name="CB4PUMA">{{cite web|url=https://censusreporter.org/profiles/79500US3604107-nyc-queens-community-district-4-elmhurst-south-corona-puma-ny/|title=NYC-Queens Community District 4--Elmhurst & South Corona PUMA, NY|publisher=Census Reporter|access-date=July 17, 2018}}</ref> In 2018, an estimated 27% of Corona and Elmhurst residents lived in poverty, compared to 19% in all of Queens and 20% in all of New York City. One in fourteen residents (7%) were unemployed, compared to 8% in Queens and 9% in New York City. Rent burden, or the percentage of residents who have difficulty paying their rent, is 62% in Corona and Elmhurst, higher than the boroughwide and citywide rates of 53% and 51%, respectively. Based on this calculation, {{as of|2018|lc=y}}, Corona and Elmhurst are considered to be high-income relative to the rest of the city and not [[gentrify]]ing.<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{Rp|7}}

As according to the 2020 census data from [[New York City Department of City Planning]], Corona had 51,500 Hispanic residents, there were between 10,000 and 19,999 Asian residents, and 5,000 to 9,000 Black residents, meanwhile the White residents were less than 5000.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/planning-level/nyc-population/census2020/dcp_2020-census-briefing-booklet-1.pdf|title=Key Population & Housing Characteristics; 2020 Census Results for New York City|publisher=[[New York City Department of City Planning]]|date=August 2021|access-date=November 7, 2021|pages=21, 25, 29, 33}}#%5B%7B%22num%22%3A235%2C%22gen%22%3A0%7D%2C%7B%22name%22%3A%22FitR%22%7D%2C-36%2C-50%2C1371%2C841%5D</ref><ref name="cnn.com">{{cite web | title=Map: Race and ethnicity across the US | website=CNN | date=August 14, 2021 | url=https://www.cnn.com/interactive/2021/us/census-race-ethnicity-map/ | access-date=November 7, 2021}}</ref>

===North Corona===
Based on data from the 2010 United States Census, the population of North Corona was 52,037, a change of 4,881 (9.4%) from the 47,156 counted in 2000. Covering an area of {{cvt|413.24|acre}}, the neighborhood had a population density of {{convert|125.9|PD/acre|PD/sqmi PD/sqkm}}.<ref name="PLP5"/>

The racial makeup of the neighborhood was 1.8% (929) White, 4.9% (2,566) African American, 0.1% (67) Native American, 6.9% (3,597) Asian, 0% (5) Pacific Islander, 0.7% (351) from other races, and 0.5% (259) from two or more races. Hispanic or Latino of any race were 85.1% (44,263) of the population.<ref name="PLP3A"/>

The 2020 census data from [[New York City Department of City Planning]] showed North Corona having between 30,000 and 39,999 Hispanic residents, meanwhile each the White, Black, and Asian residents were all each less than 5,000 residents.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/planning-level/nyc-population/census2020/dcp_2020-census-briefing-booklet-1.pdf|title=Key Population & Housing Characteristics; 2020 Census Results for New York City|publisher=[[New York City Department of City Planning]]|date=August 2021|access-date=November 7, 2021|pages=21, 25, 29, 33}}</ref><ref name="cnn.com"/>

==Police and crime==
Corona is patrolled by the 110th and 115th Precincts of the [[New York City Police Department]] (NYPD), located at 94-41 43rd Avenue and 92-15 Northern Boulevard, respectively.<ref name="NYPD 110th Precinct">{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/site/nypd/bureaus/patrol/precincts/110th-precinct.page|title=NYPD – 110th Precinct|website=www.nyc.gov|publisher=[[New York City Police Department]]|access-date=October 3, 2016}}</ref> The 110th Precinct ranked 15th safest out of 69 patrol areas for per-capita crime in 2010.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/crime-safety-report/queens/corona/|title=Corona and Elmhurst – DNAinfo.com Crime and Safety Report|website=www.dnainfo.com|access-date=October 6, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170415063655/https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/crime-safety-report/queens/corona|archive-date=April 15, 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref> {{As of|2018}}, with a non-fatal assault rate of 34 per 100,000 people, Corona's rate of [[violent crime]]s per capita is less than that of the city as a whole. The incarceration rate of 227 per 100,000 people is lower than that of the city as a whole.<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{Rp|8}}

The 110th Precinct has a lower crime rate than in the 1990s, with crimes across all categories having decreased by 83.2% between 1990 and 2020. The precinct reported four murders, 29 rapes, 270 robberies, 359 felony assaults, 196 burglaries, 485 grand larcenies, and 138 grand larcenies auto in 2020.<ref>{{cite web|title=110th Precinct CompStat Report|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/nypd/downloads/pdf/crime_statistics/cs-en-us-110pct.pdf|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180413193406/http://www1.nyc.gov:80/assets/nypd/downloads/pdf/crime_statistics/cs-en-us-110pct.pdf |archive-date=April 13, 2018 |access-date=January 18, 2021|website=www.nyc.gov|publisher=[[New York City Police Department]]}}</ref>

==Health==
{{As of|2018}}, [[preterm birth]]s are less common in Corona and Elmhurst than in other places citywide, but births to teenage mothers are more common. In Corona and Elmhurst, there were 83 preterm births per 1,000 live births (compared to 87 per 1,000 citywide), and 25.8 births to teenage mothers per 1,000 live births (compared to 19.3 per 1,000 citywide).<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{Rp|11}} Corona and Elmhurst have a high population of residents who are [[Health insurance coverage in the United States|uninsured]]. In 2018, this population of uninsured residents was estimated to be 25%, which is higher than the citywide rate of 12%.<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{Rp|14}}

The concentration of [[fine particulate matter]], the deadliest type of [[air pollutant]], in Corona and Elmhurst is {{convert|0.0077|mg/m3|oz/ft3}}, slightly higher than the city average.<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{Rp|9}} Fifteen percent of Corona and Elmhurst residents are [[Smoking|smokers]], which is slightly higher than the city average of 14% of residents being smokers.<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{Rp|13}} In Corona and Elmhurst, 20% of residents are [[obese]], 9% are [[diabetic]], and 23% have [[high blood pressure]]—compared to the citywide averages of 20%, 14%, and 24%, respectively.<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{Rp|16}} In addition, 24% of children are obese, compared to the citywide average of 20%.<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{Rp|12}}

Eighty-eight percent of residents eat some fruits and vegetables every day, which is slightly higher than the city's average of 87%. In 2018, 68% of residents described their health as "good", "very good", or "excellent", lower than the city's average of 78%.<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{Rp|13}} For every supermarket in Corona and Elmhurst, there are 16 [[convenience store|bodegas]].<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{Rp|10}}

The [[Elmhurst Hospital Center]] is located in Elmhurst.<ref>{{cite web | last=Finkel | first=Beth | title=Guide To Queens Hospitals | website=Queens Tribune | date=February 27, 2014 | url=http://queenstribune.com/guide-to-queens-hospitals/ | access-date=March 7, 2019 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170204185507/http://queenstribune.com/guide-to-queens-hospitals/ | archive-date=February 4, 2017 | url-status=dead }}</ref>

===Incidents===
In 2020, the neighborhoods of Corona, [[East Elmhurst, Queens|East Elmhurst]], [[Elmhurst, Queens|Elmhurst]], and [[Jackson Heights, Queens|Jackson Heights]] were most affected by the [[COVID-19 pandemic in New York City]].<ref>{{Cite news|last1=Correal|first1=Annie|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/04/09/nyregion/coronavirus-queens-corona-jackson-heights-elmhurst.html|title='A Tragedy Is Unfolding': Inside New York's Virus Epicenter|date=April 9, 2020|work=The New York Times|access-date=April 9, 2020|last2=Jacobs|first2=Andrew|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|last3=Jones|first3=Ryan Christopher}}</ref> {{As of|2020|August|10|alt=As of August 10}}, these communities, with a cumulative 303,494 residents, had recorded 12,954 COVID-19 cases and 1,178 deaths.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/site/doh/covid/covid-19-data.page|title=COVID-19 Data by ZIP Code of Residence|date=August 10, 2020|work=City of New York|access-date=August 10, 2020|language=en-US}}</ref> COVID-19 cases in ZIP Codes 11368 and 11369 were the highest of any ZIP Code in New York City.<ref>{{cite web | last=Brand | first=David | title=COVID rates in six Queens zip codes reveal lethal impact on communities of color | website=Queens Daily Eagle | date=May 19, 2020 | url=https://queenseagle.com/all/covid-rates-in-six-queens-zip-codes-reveal-grim-impact-on-communities-of-color | access-date=June 14, 2020}}</ref>

== Education ==
Corona and Elmhurst generally have a lower ratio of college-educated residents than the rest of the city {{as of|2018|lc=y}}. While 28% of residents age 25 and older have a college education or higher, 30% have less than a high school education and 42% are high school graduates or have some college education. By contrast, 39% of Queens residents and 43% of city residents have a college education or higher.<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{Rp|6}} The percentage of Corona and Elmhurst students excelling in math rose from 36% in 2000 to 66% in 2011, and reading achievement rose from 42% to 49% during the same time period.<ref name=":17">{{Cite web|url=http://furmancenter.org/files/sotc/QN_04_11.pdf|title=Elmhurst/Corona – QN 04|date=2011|publisher=[[Furman Center for Real Estate and Urban Policy]]|access-date=October 5, 2016}}</ref>

Corona and Elmhurst's rate of elementary school student absenteeism is less than the rest of New York City. In Corona and Elmhurst, 11% of elementary school students missed twenty or more days per [[school year]], lower than the citywide average of 20%.<ref name=":21"/>{{Rp|24 (PDF p. 55)}}<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{Rp|6}} Additionally, 81% of high school students in Corona and Elmhurst graduate on time, more than the citywide average of 75%.<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{Rp|6}}

==== Black Heritage Reference Center of Queens County ====
Corona also houses one of the most extensive collections of African-American art and literature in the Langston Hughes Community Library and Cultural Center, which serves Queens with reference and circulating collections, totaling approximately 30,000 volumes of materials written about or relating to black culture. The '''Black Heritage Reference Center of Queens County''' includes books, periodicals, theses and dissertations, VHS videos, cassettes and CDs, photographs, posters, prints, paintings, and sculpture. Cultural arts programs are scheduled through the center. Meeting space is available to community organizations by application. Special features of the Center include:<ref>{{cite web | title=Black Heritage Reference Center | website=Queens Public Library | url=https://www.queenslibrary.org/research/special-collections/black-heritage-reference-center | access-date=April 12, 2020}}</ref>
* The Schomburg Clippings File, an extensive microfiche collection of periodicals, magazine clippings, typescripts, broadsides, pamphlets, programs, book reviews, menus and ephemera of all kinds.
* The UMI Thesis and Dissertation Collection consists of more than 1,000 volumes of doctoral and master dissertations concerning the African and African-American diasporas.
* The Adele Cohen Music Collection contains most of America's foremost black publications on microfilm. The papers cover 15 states beginning in 1893, and are updated each year with current issues.
* The Black Heritage Video Collection documents the history and culture of Africans and African-Americans on tape, and in all subject areas including literature, biography, social science, fine arts.

== Transportation ==
The [[New York City Subway]]'s [[IRT Flushing Line]] ({{NYCS trains|Flushing}}) runs through the neighborhood with stops at [[Mets–Willets Point station (IRT Flushing Line)|Mets–Willets Point]], [[111th Street (IRT Flushing Line)|111th Street]], [[103rd Street–Corona Plaza (IRT Flushing Line)|103rd Street–Corona Plaza]], and [[Junction Boulevard (IRT Flushing Line)|Junction Boulevard]].<ref>{{NYCS const|map}}</ref> The {{NYC bus link|Q14|Q23|Q58|Q63|Q66|Q72|Q88|Q90|Q98|prose=y}} buses also serve the neighborhood.<ref>{{Cite NYC bus map|Q}}</ref>

The area was formerly served by the [[Long Island Rail Road]]'s [[Corona station (LIRR)|Corona station]] on the [[Port Washington Branch]], but this closed in 1964. As of 2025, the closest active station, further to the east in [[Flushing Meadows–Corona Park]], is [[Mets–Willets Point (LIRR station)]]

==In popular culture==
* Books about Corona's history and present include Roger Sanjek's ''The Future of Us All'' and Steven Gregory's ''Black Corona''.
* Chapter 6 of [[Andrew Morton (writer)|Andrew Morton]]'s biography ''Madonna'' describes American pop singer [[Madonna]]'s brief stint as a Corona resident in the late 1970s and early '80s.
* [[F. Scott Fitzgerald]] referred to the [[Flushing Meadows–Corona Park]] dumps as the "valley of ashes" in his novel ''[[The Great Gatsby]]''.
* [[Paul Simon]] referred to a fictional character as "Rosie, the queen of Corona" in his 1972 song ''[[Me and Julio Down by the Schoolyard]]''.
* Lemon Ice King of Corona appears in the opening credits of the TV show ''[[The King of Queens]]''.<ref name=":0"/>
* [[Archie Bunker]] of ''[[All in the Family]]'', at fictional 704 Hauser Street.<ref>[[Sam Roberts (newspaper journalist)|Roberts, Sam]]. [https://www.nytimes.com/1993/12/19/arts/the-cranky-spirit-of-archie-bunker-haunts-this-house.html "The Cranky Spirit Of Archie Bunker Haunts This House"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180810074300/https://www.nytimes.com/1993/12/19/arts/the-cranky-spirit-of-archie-bunker-haunts-this-house.html |date=August 10, 2018 }}, ''[[The New York Times]]'', December 19, 1993. Accessed August 9, 2018. "Mr. Lear, who only occasionally passes through Queens on his way to or from the city's airports, wasn't much help in identifying Archie's old neighborhood, but Sean Dwyer, director of development at Mr. Lear's production company, Act III Communications, unequivocally ruled out Glendale, Ridgewood, Woodside, Maspeth, Astoria and several other candidates and pinpointed the likely locale as Corona. 'I talked to a schoolteacher and one of the writers, whose mother lives in Corona,' Mr. Dwyer said. 'It used to be white middle class. Now it's racially mixed: white, Jewish, black, Indian, Latinos. Number 704 Hauser Street is in Corona.'"</ref>
